passages.happening:
‘When I heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim will be exposed, as well as the crimes of Samaria’ (verse 1). They practice deceit. Thieves break into houses, and bandits raid in the streets. They do not consider that God remembers all their evil, and their deeds now surround them (verse 2).

They please the king with their wickedness and the princes with their lies (verse 3). They are all adulterers, like an oven a baker leaves to burn while the dough rises (verse 4). On the king's day the princes are inflamed with wine (verse 5). ‘For they prepare their heart like an oven while they lie in wait; all night their anger smolders; in the morning it blazes like a flaming fire’ (verse 6). They devour their rulers. ‘All their kings fall; not one of them calls upon Me’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The chapter reflects the chaos after Jeroboam II died, about 753 BC. In the next thirty years Israel had six kings, and four of them were murdered. Shallum killed Jeroboam's son Zechariah after six months. Menahem killed Shallum after one month. Pekah, an officer, murdered Menahem's son Pekahiah, and Hoshea in turn killed Pekah. The princes drunk at the king's feast and the plotters who devour their rulers fit that pattern of palace coups.

The household oven was a clay cylinder in which a fire burned down to embers, and bread dough was slapped onto its hot walls. A baker might bank the fire overnight while the dough rose and stir it to full heat in the morning. That is the picture: plotters whose passion smolders all night and blazes at dawn.

The saddest line is the last. Kings fall one after another, and not one of them calls on God. Even when God moves to heal, the healing only shows how deep the sickness runs.
passages.later: Second Kings tells the murders one after another (2 Kings 15:8-30). Long before, the people had asked Samuel for a king to lead them like the nations (1 Samuel 8:5).
passages.asks: Not one of the kings called on God. Ask where in your own life you plan and plot without asking him. And ask what anger has been smoldering in you overnight that could blaze in the morning.

passages.t: A half-baked cake and a senseless dove
passages.happening:
‘Ephraim mixes with the nations; Ephraim is an unturned cake’ (verse 8). Foreigners eat up his strength, ‘but he does not notice. Even his hair is streaked with gray, but he does not know’ (verse 9). His pride testifies against him, and still he does not return to the LORD or seek him (verse 10).

‘So Ephraim has become like a silly, senseless dove’ (verse 11), calling to Egypt and then turning to Assyria. As they go, God will spread his net over them and bring them down like birds (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
An unturned cake was flatbread baked on hot stones or embers and never flipped, burned on one side and raw on the other, good for nothing. Ephraim has mixed itself into the nations and become neither one thing nor the other.

Gray hair spreading without notice was a sign of age and decline. Israel is growing old and weak and does not see it. The dove, easily lured and easily frightened, flying back and forth, was a proverb for foolishness, and the net was the bird-catcher's tool.

Calling to Egypt, then turning to Assyria sums up those years. Menahem paid tribute to Tiglath-pileser III, called Pul in 2 Kings 15:19, to keep his throne. Pekah joined an alliance against Assyria and lost much of his land. Hoshea submitted to Assyria, then sent to So king of Egypt for help and stopped paying tribute, which led to the siege and fall of Samaria.
passages.later: Hoshea sent envoys to So king of Egypt and stopped paying tribute, and Assyria put him in prison and besieged Samaria (2 Kings 17:3-6). Isaiah warned Judah in the same way: ‘Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help’ (Isaiah 31:1).
passages.asks: Ephraim's hair turned gray and he did not know. Ask what kind of decline happens so slowly in a person that it goes unnoticed. And ask where you tend to look for safety when you are afraid.

passages.t: They turn, but not to the Most High
passages.happening:
‘Woe to them, for they have strayed from Me’ is how verse 13 begins. Destruction is coming, because they have rebelled. ‘Though I would redeem them, they speak lies against Me’ (verse 13).

They do not cry out to God from their hearts when they wail on their beds. They cut themselves for grain and new wine, and turn away from him (verse 14). He trained and strengthened their arms, and they plot evil against him (verse 15). ‘They turn, but not to the Most High; they are like a faulty bow’ (verse 16). Their leaders will fall by the sword, and they will be mocked in Egypt.
passages.hearers:
The section opens with woe, the cry of a funeral lament. Verse 13 holds the heart of the chapter: God wants to redeem them, and they answer with lies.

In verse 14 the standard Hebrew text reads they gather themselves, but many manuscripts and the Greek translation read they slash themselves, which the BSB follows. On that reading the people cut themselves as they pray for grain and wine, a mourning and worship practice tied to the worship of Baal and forbidden to Israel. They treat the LORD like the fertility gods, as a power to be moved by their pain, not a God to be known. They wail on their beds, but they do not cry out to him.

A faulty bow looks like a weapon but throws its arrow wide. Israel turns this way and that, but never to the one place that would help. The chapter is built from pictures, an oven, a cake, gray hair, a dove, a net and a bow, and running through them all is a failure to notice, to know and to cry out.
passages.later: On Mount Carmel the prophets of Baal cut themselves as they called on their god (1 Kings 18:28), and the law forbade Israel that practice (Deuteronomy 14:1).
passages.asks: They wailed on their beds but did not cry out to God. Ask what the difference is between complaining about trouble and bringing it to him. And ask where you have turned in many directions, but not to the Most High.
